[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced Routing in Ruby on Rails: Constraints, Scopes, and Concerns"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"As Ruby on Rails applications grow in scale and complexity, managing routes efficiently becomes critical. Default resourceful routing is often insufficient for enterprise-grade applications. Rails provides advanced routing mechanisms such as constraints, scopes, and concerns to keep your config/routes.rb file clean, maintainable, and robust."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Route Constraints"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Route constraints allow you to restrict requests based on specific conditions such as regular expressions, request attributes, or custom objects. This is particularly useful for API versioning, subdomain routing, or security enforcement."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"Rails.application.routes.draw do
  # Restricting an ID to numeric values only
  resources :users, constraints: { id: /[0-9]+/ }

  # Subdomain routing constraint
  namespace :admin, constraints: { subdomain: 'admin' } do
    resources :dashboard
  end
end"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can also create advanced constraints using custom Ruby objects by implementing the matches? method. This allows you to encapsulate complex logic like session inspection or IP whitelisting."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"class WhitelistedIpConstraint
  def initialize
    @allowed_ips = ['127.0.0.1', '192.168.1.1']
  end

  def matches?(request)
    @allowed_ips.include?(request.remote_ip)
  end
end

Rails.application.routes.draw do
  constraints(WhitelistedIpConstraint.new) do
    namespace :admin do
      resources :system_logs
    end
  end
end"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Advanced Scopes"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Scopes let you set common routing options for a group of routes without altering the URL path or the generated helper names in the same way namespaces do. You can scope by module, path prefix, constraints, or defaults."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"Rails.application.routes.draw do
  # Scoping paths and modules simultaneously
  scope '(locale)', locale: /en|es|fr/ do
    resources :articles
    resources :comments
  end

  # Changing the URL path prefix while keeping the controller unchanged
  scope path: '/api/v1', module: 'api/v1' do
    resources :posts, only: [:index, :show]
  end
end"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Routing Concerns"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"Routing concerns allow you to declare common routes that can be reused inside other resources and namespaces. This adheres to the DRY principle (Don't Repeat Yourself) when multiple resources share common nested routes, such as comments or images."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"Rails.application.routes.draw do
  concern :commentable do
    resources :comments, only: [:index, :create]
  end

  concern :imageable do
    resources :images, only: [:index, :create, :destroy]
  end

  # Applying concerns to multiple resources
  resources :posts, concerns: [:commentable, :imageable]
  resources :messages, concerns: [:commentable]
end"},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Large Rails Applications"},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Organize large route files by splitting them into separate files within config/routes/ and loading them using Dir[Rails.root.join('config', 'routes', '*.rb')]."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use route constraints sparingly to prevent performance bottlenecks during request routing dispatch."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Leverage concerns when you have identical nested resource blocks across three or more controllers."},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"By mastering constraints, scopes, and concerns, you can maintain a clean, highly structured, and scalable routing layer in your Ruby on Rails applications."}]
